module


public import Mathlib.Algebra.GCDMonoid.Finset
public import Mathlib.Order.Interval.Finset.Defs

@[expose] public section

namespace Finset

/-- The least common multiple of ${n+1, \dotsc, n+k}$. -/
def lcmInterval {α : Type*} [CommSemiring α] [NormalizedGCDMonoid α]
    [Preorder α] [LocallyFiniteOrder α] (n k : α) : α := (Finset.Ioc n (n + k)).lcm id

end Finset

findings.description: The docstring at line 26 describes the LCM of the consecutive terms {n+1, …, n+k}, but the polymorphic definition computes the LCM of the order interval (n,n+k]. The assumptions do not connect the preorder to addition or make addition by 1 the successor operation. These descriptions agree over the intended ℕ, but not in general. In scratch Lean, equipping ℕᵒᵈ with the transported natural-number NormalizedGCDMonoid gives lcmInterval (2 : ℕᵒᵈ) 1 = 1, whereas the LCM of the singleton {2+1} is 3. The interval definition itself is coherent, and all current consumers use ℕ correctly; this is a documentation-scope issue.
findings.source_evidence: Mathlib/Order/Interval/Finset/Defs.lean specifies membership in Ioc n (n+k) as n < x ∧ x ≤ n+k, with no arithmetic compatibility in LocallyFiniteOrder. Mathlib/Order/Interval/Finset/Nat.lean proves the natural-number specialization Ioc n (n+1) = {n+1}. Erdős, Some Unconventional Problems in Number Theory (1979), p. 67, defines M(n;k) using the integers n+i for 1 ≤ i ≤ k: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-22.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the generic operation as 'The normalized least common multiple of the order interval `(n, n + k]`.' Then add that, for α = ℕ, this is the LCM of {n+1, …, n+k}. No change to the definition or its current consumers is necessary.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/678.lean, line 58 says M(36,8) > M(48,9), but the correctly proved statement at line 62 uses lcmInterval 47 9. The docstring's inequality is false: Lean computes M(36,8) = 148875406680, M(47,9) = 68183715600, and M(48,9) = 647745298200. Both the stated Lean inequality and the negation of the docstring's inequality were independently verified with `by decide`.
findings.source_evidence: Cambie, Resolution of an Erdős' problem on least common multiples, arXiv:2410.09138v1, Introduction, explicitly gives lcm{37,…,44} > lcm{48,…,56}. With M(n,k) = lcm{n+1,…,n+k}, this is M(36,8) > M(47,9), exactly as in the Lean statement. Source: https://arxiv.org/e-print/2410.09138.
findings.suggested_fix: Change M(48,9) to M(47,9) in the docstring; leave the proved Lean statement unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The Lean variant counts triples (k,m,n), while the accompanying explanation also describes infinitely many pairs (m,n) with a suitable k allowed to vary.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The projection (k,m,n) ↦ (m,n) has exactly the admissible pairs as its image. Each fiber is finite: n+k ≤ m implies k ≤ m, so a fixed pair permits only finitely many natural-number values of k. Consequently the admissible triples are infinite if and only if the admissible pairs are infinite. This equivalence was proved for the actual predicates in /workspace/review/infinitude_equivalence.lean.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalization was found in the intended natural-number definition or its problem statements. Scratch Lean proves agreement with `(Finset.range k).lcm (fun i => n+i+1)`, the corresponding divisibility characterization, positivity over ℕ, and agreement with Nat.lcmUpto when n=0. Tests cover k=0 (value 1), k=1, integer intervals containing zero or having negative length, and the one-element semiring. All final experiments compiled, and the target file remains unchanged at the specified commit. The sources confirm that 677 is open and 678 is proved in Lean; the main 678 statement captures the explicitly cited all-sufficiently-large-k result, not infinitude for a fixed k. The full 1992 Eureka article was not recovered, but the relevant meaning and quantifier distinction were independently verified from the current source pages, Erdős's 1979 paper, and Cambie's LaTeX source.
